At that time, the World-Honored One went to inquire after his illness. [The commentary] says: From this point downward is the ninth section, in which Rāhula is commanded;
it consists of the initial command and the subsequent refusal. This is the initial command. "Rāhula" [means...]
Regarding "Cloud-Grasper-Sun" (Yúnzhí Rì): this is originally the name of the asura Grasping-the-Sun (Zhírì Āxiūluó), who is the asura king Rāhu mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This is the vanguard of the non-gods; when the non-god generals fight with Śakra, he serves as their front-line army.

When people see the Son of Heaven, the Sun and Moon, emitting light that shoots afar, they think it is the eye of a non-deva; yet it is not a non-deva, for he merely grasps the sun with his hand to obscure its light.
Now, this Son of the Buddha takes this as a metaphor for his name, and it is likewise so.
The Buddha-dharma is like the sun; because of this son, the light of the sun of my Buddha-dharma’s wisdom is obstructed, just as by the asuras, and thus he was named after them.

His ancient name was "Born in the Palace" (Kongsheng). When Yaśodharā was slandered, she made a vow to clear her name, asserting that the child was truly born in the palace and was not the offspring of another outside man; therefore, he was named "Born in the Palace."

The causes and conditions regarding this child are explained at length in the sūtras: because in a former life he was a king who would not grant an audience to a śramaṇa who sought to see him for six days;
or because he blocked a rat's hole for six days, thereby obstructing a mother and her child from obtaining food, he remained within the womb for six years.

Later, when the Buddha arrived at the kingdom of Kapilavastu, he manifested a thousand bhikṣus whose forms resembled his own over the course of seven days, and sent them to select the Buddha; they indeed reached the Buddha’s location, thereby clearly identifying him as the Son of the Buddha.
He then commissioned Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to deliver him; at that time [the boy] was still young, so I shall not record the details for fear of prolixity.
After some time, Rāhula arrived there to inquire after his illness.
The commentary says:
There are three subsequent sections; this one generally describes the failure of the Way.
Previously, the praise of leaving home concerned the conditioned and the phenomenal.
Those who had left the household life challenged him with the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
When he interrogated the laypeople with the truth, their path was blocked and their words exhausted; thus, they were unable to withstand him.
The Sūtra says: "For what reason? ... up to ... the meritorious benefits."
The commentary states:
Below, the ultimate principle is revealed; first there is the inquiry, followed by the revelation.
Within the revelation, there are further two parts:
First, the matter at hand is set forth; second, the words of others are revealed.
Regarding the matter at hand, there are two parts:
first, the question posed by others is revealed; second, one's own response is revealed.
This inquiry and the subsequent manifestation serve to clarify the question of others.
These youths are of the Brahmin caste and belong to the Licchavi clan.
Since the Buddha was a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) and Rāhula was his successor, they are now praised as being likewise Wheel-turning Kings.

There are four types of wheel-turning monarchs—those of iron, copper, silver, and gold—each capable of ruling over one, two, three, or four continents of human beings, as distinguished in the standard classifications.
Having already cast off the jewels of the Cakravartin emperor and become a renunciant, what benefit is there in studying the merits of renunciation?
The Sūtra says: "I shall, according to the Dharma, attain the supreme benefits of merit."
The commentary states: This clarifies that [the question] has already been answered.
The life of one who has left the household is vast and expansive like empty space; the life of one remaining at home is constricting and pressing, comparable to a prison.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Though the peacock has colors that adorn its body, it cannot fly as far as the wild goose or the crane.
Though the white-robed layperson possesses the power of wealth and status, they are not as superior as the merit of one who has left the household life."
"Merit" refers to the arising of goodness; "victory" refers to the cessation of evil.
Merit is blessing; victory is named wisdom.
Victory is that which can transcend the world; merit consists of the two adornments of blessing and wisdom.
[Sūtra]: After some time, Vimalakīrti arrived and spoke these words.
[Commentary]: This section below reveals the words of another.
There are two parts:
first, the presentation of the ultimate method; second, the formal presentation of the discourse.
This is the initial section.
Sūtra: From "Only Rāhula" to "the Victorious Merits of Virtue.
Commentary: Below is the formal presentation of the discourse.
There are five parts:

first, the formal presentation of the reasoning and interrogation; second, the exhortation for him to leave the household life; third, the youth’s inquiry; fourth, Vimala’s instruction; and fifth, the youth’s attainment of benefit.
The beginning consists of three parts:
first, a general negation; second, a specific interrogation; and third, a formal conclusion.
This is the initial passage.
Sūtra: "Why is this so? To reach this state is what constitutes 'leaving home' (pravrajyā). Commentary:
Within the subsequent detailed interrogation, there are two parts: first, the citation, and second, the elucidation.
This is the first point.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness:

whereas the preceding section praised renunciation as having conventional characteristics, the present section takes ultimate signlessness as its criterion; therefore, it states that there is no benefit and no merit.
The *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā* states:
"Conventional phenomena are the branches, while ultimate reality is the root.
The preceding praise of renunciation was a praise of the conventional as being secondary.
Now, taking the fundamental principle as the standard, it is said that one who possesses no benefit or merit is truly a renunciant.
[The Sūtra] begins with "O Rāhula" and concludes with "the benefits and merits.
The commentary states:

The following section reveals three aspects: first, it clarifies the renunciation of the conditioned with signs; second, it clarifies the renunciation of the unconditioned without signs; and finally, it clarifies the benefits and virtues of Mahāyāna renunciation.
This is the first passage.

Regarding the aforementioned essence and characteristics of the merit and benefits for others, these pertain to the conditioned and possess signs; they are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Sūtra: "Now, as for those who have gone forth... up to "...the merit and benefits."
The commentary states:
This clarifies the unconditioned and signless renunciation.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
Now, those who have left the household life fundamentally seek to eliminate the marks of the mundane world and aspire toward the ultimate reality of unconditioned emptiness of nature.
Within this emptiness of nature, what benefit or merit could there be?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Meaning of Reason) states:

All noble ones (*ārya*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet there are distinctions among them. The unconditioned refers to nirvāṇa-liberation, the principle of suchness-extinction, and the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This is because nirvāṇa-liberation severs the bonds of birth and death; suchness is profoundly tranquil and free from delusion and inversion; and the nature of analytical cessation is free from the two supreme obstacles.
One leaves the household life for the sake of seeking this, because it is the root of all virtues.
It is not for the sake of the conditioned, because that is not the root of virtue.
Therefore, in the unconditioned, there is neither virtue nor benefit.

Within the fundamental unconditioned, there is no differentiation; its nature, characteristics, and qualities are likewise without differentiation. Its functional efficacy and excellence are not devoid of the excellence of immutability.
Furthermore, one who has left the household life is free from discriminative clinging;
to possess virtue or gain is discriminative and is not true renunciation.
Therefore, true renunciation breaks through discriminative clinging, being without virtue and without gain.
Sūtra: "Only Rāhula [attains] the formless, which is not form.
Commentary: The following clarifies the twenty-four points regarding the benefits of the Mahāyāna renunciant life.

The original version contained twenty-two phrases, which entirely lacked the sections on "neither form nor non-form" and "the absence of all grasping" found in the new version; furthermore, within the section on the dual cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, it was missing the practice of vipaśyanā, and within the section on abandoning evil and cultivating good, it lacked the practice of cultivating good.
Regarding these three phrases, the meaning of the principle of emptiness is as follows:
within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is no "other" or "that," no "this" or "from here," nor is there anything in between;
it is far removed from all views, and there is no distinction between form and formlessness.
The *Yingliyi* (Principles of Reason) states:

Among these three phrases, "neither self nor other" means that for one who has left the household life, both person and self are discarded; there is no "other" or "that" outside of oneself, for others are embraced as identical to oneself, and one constantly practices their deliverance.
Externally, there is nothing beyond this; for when another attains happiness, it is as if I myself have attained it.
Nor is there an intermediate state existing apart from "thing" and "self.
These two distances all views, and the five views are completely severed.

The old translation says "sixty-two views," but these are subsumed solely under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and thus their characteristics are extremely narrow.

Regarding the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are non-form; "form" refers to the cultivation and adornment of physical appearance, while "non-form" refers to consciousness, discernment, and understanding. Since they do not possess any of this, they are termed "non-existent" (*arūpa*).
Alternatively, it is because non-Buddhists with false views either cling to the self as being form, clinging to the aggregate of form as the self;
or they cling to the self as being non-form, clinging to the four aggregates and the life-faculty as the real self.
Among the sixty-two views, those who hold that the self is material and possesses perception after death,
or that the self is immaterial and possesses perception after death, and so forth— all such as these have left the household life for what is unconditioned.
Therefore, one abandons all that is non-virtuous and accords with the correct views; the following sections should be understood accordingly.
Sūtra: "This is the path to nirvāṇa, embraced by the Noble Ones. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
This consists of three phrases.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness:
that which is neither this nor that, nor anything in between, is able to reach nirvana; therefore, it is called the "path."
Because it penetrates all views, it is praised by the wise.
Because it is neither form nor non-form, it is embraced by the noble ones.
The meaning that accords with reason is as follows:
Those who have gone forth for the sake of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) do so for three reasons: first, to reach nirvāṇa; second, because they are praised by the noble ones;
and third, because they are embraced by the noble practices. The noble ones constantly embrace and lead them, regarding them as supreme.
The old translation says, "abiding in nirvāṇa"; by taking this as the path, one is able to abide in nirvāṇa.
It also says, "the sphere of the noble ones' practice," meaning it is praised by the noble ones because it accords with their enlightened minds.
Sūtra: From "subduing all māras" to "being free from all evil dharmas.
Commentary: This consists of seven phrases.
The *Kongliyi* states:

Because they conceptually cling to existence, they become the various māras; they enter the five destinies, fail to attain the five eyes, and lack the power of the five faculties. Thus, they harm sentient beings while their own evil ceases not.

If one has left the household life for the sake of realizing emptiness, the various Māras will naturally be subdued; this is explained at length, concluding that one’s own evils will cease. The meaning according to the principle is as follows:

for one who has left the household life for the sake of unconditioned dharmas, (1) the four Māras are subdued; (2) the five destinies are transcended; (3) the five eyes are attained; (4) the five faculties are established; (5) the five powers are acquired; (6) all sentient beings are not harmed or afflicted; and (7) one is able to abandon all of one’s own evils.

As for the five eyes: first is the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which is not produced through the cultivation of meditative concentration; its nature is pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements.
Second is the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), which is produced as a result of cultivation; it is pure matter derived from the four great elements.
Third is the Dharma-eye, which possesses wisdom that takes the teachings as its object.
Fourth is the Wisdom-eye, which is the knowledge of emptiness that takes principle as its object.
Fifth is the Buddha-eye, the sublime wisdom that discerns both self and others.
The remaining four māras, the five destinies, and the faculties and powers are all as previously explained.
The Sūtra says: "He subdues all non-Buddhists... up to being free from 'I' and 'mine'.
The Commentary says:
This consists of six propositions.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

if one leaves the household life for the sake of existence or with the perception of existence, one cannot defeat the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or transcend conventional designations (*prajñapti*), and so forth, up to being unable to abandon the notions of "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*).
If one leaves the household life for the sake of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and signlessness (*animitta*), one thereby subdues the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and abandons "I" and "mine.
The meaning according to principle is as follows:

those who leave the household life for the sake of unconditioned phenomena—first, because of right view, they subdue the non-Buddhists; second, because the essence of dharmas transcends words, they transcend provisional names; third, by attaining great *nirvāṇa*, they emerge from the mire of craving; fourth, because there is no attachment, there is no bondage; fifth, because there is no substance of self or other, there is nothing to be grasped.
The old translation reverses this, stating: "Because there is nothing received, one is detached from 'I' and 'mine'.
[The sūtra says: "There are no various graspings, up to and including the excellent protection of the minds of others.
The commentary states:
This consists of three phrases.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness:
"grasping" (upādāna) refers to the sense of conceptualizing and clinging.
"Disturbance" means vexation;
"disorder" means affliction;
"regulation" means subduing.
The protectors provide protection accordingly.

For those who have gone forth for the sake of the emptiness of the unconditioned, there is no grasping, freedom from afflictions, subduing of one’s own mind, and the cessation of the intent to protect others.
Those who have left the household life for the sake of the characteristics of the conditioned cannot act in this way.
The meaning that accords with principle is as follows:
first, to be free from all grasping.
"Grasping" (upādāna) signifies the meaning of covetous attachment and clinging; its essence consists of four types of grasping:
first, grasping at sense-objects (kāmopādāna), which is craving for the five sensory realms;
second, grasping at views (dṛṣṭyupādāna), which is the adherence to various views.
Third is the clinging to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which clings to various precepts;
fourth is the clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*), which clings to a distinct, real self.
Since there is no essence of a self and there is only a name, this "name" is called the clinging to the doctrine of self.
The latter three consist of the essence of wisdom; as their names indicate, each takes its own insight as its intrinsic nature.
This is free from all grasping;
it is the path of subduing.
It severs all grasping and severs the path of delusion.
There are two kinds of non-distraction.

Regarding "distraction": "distraction" (*ra*) has the meaning of dispersal, while "scattering" (*la*) means agitation; that is, the essence itself is scattered, the mind rushes toward objects, and because it is agitated and unsettled, it is called "distraction."
Alternatively, there are six types of distraction: first, intrinsic; second, characteristic; third, coarse heaviness; fourth, internal; fifth, external; and sixth, mental attention.
There are three ways to regulate one's own mind and protect the minds of others.
One skillfully subdues the afflictions of one’s own mind and protects the minds of others so that they do not give rise to distress, thereby bringing them to fulfillment.
This is the sutra on following *śamatha* up to the cultivation of all virtues.
The commentary states:
This consists of two phrases.

First, "cultivating wisdom in accordance with meditative concentration": "quiescence" (śamatha) refers to concentration, and "insight" (vipaśyanā) refers to wisdom; these two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā encompass all meritorious qualities.
Second, to distance oneself from evil and cultivate goodness is called true renunciation.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness:
when one contemplates and penetrates the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the mind dwells permanently therein, it is therefore called *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Knowing the conventional and realizing the ultimate is therefore called "abandoning and cultivating.
The Sūtra says: "If one can act in this way, it is called true renunciation.
The Commentary states:
This is the correct interpretation of the sutra.
At that time, Vimalakīrti arrived and said, "It would be fitting for us all to leave the household life together.
The commentary states:
The following is the second section, which exhorts one to practice the life of renunciation.
It consists of an initial general exhortation followed by an explanation of the reasons for this exhortation;
this is the first part of that section.
The Buddha-dharma accords with reality; therefore, it is called "well-spoken.
*Vinaya* means "discipline" (*dāmoda*), which refers to the extensive root Vinaya.
Leaving the household life is that which is sustained by the discipline of the Buddha-dharma; thus, one is exhorted to leave the household life in accordance with the Vinaya.
This is indeed the Mahāyāna Vinaya.
As for the reason why [it is] "the foremost and most difficult," the commentary states:
This reveals the reasons for exhortation, as there are four difficulties:

first, the difficulty of a Buddha appearing in the world; second, the difficulty of being free from the eight states of non-leisure; third, the difficulty of obtaining a human body; and fourth, the difficulty of possessing the full leisure.
Now that you have obtained this leisure, it may be called a meritorious attainment; you should leave the household life.
Previously, there were no [provisions for] the latter three.
According to the *Sūtra on the Various Boys*, it is said that they could not leave the household life.
The commentary states:
Third is the youth’s inquiry.
Among the various prohibitions and obstacles, if one does not have the permission of one's parents, one cannot leave the household life.
"It is not that my original heart did not delight in leaving the household life.
[From the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, from the words "Vimalakīrti said" until "attaining the nature of a bhikṣu. Commentary:
Fourth, regarding the stainless instruction on renunciation, there are two types:
first, physical renunciation, which consists of donning the dyed robes;
second, mental renunciation, which consists of generating the resolve to practice.
To resolve to practice is true renunciation; to uphold the prohibitive precepts is to achieve the nature of a bhikṣu;
to wear the dyed robes is to assume the appearance of a bhikṣu.
I now exhort you to renounce the world, for this is based on true renunciation.
Sūtra: After thirty-two years had passed, he vowed to cultivate correct practice. Commentary:
Fifth, the benefits obtained by the youth.
After some time, I remained silent and went to visit him to inquire about his illness.
Vimalakīrti said:
"I shall conclude my response; please withdraw with humble courtesy."
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One went to inquire after his illness.
He praised him, saying:
"From this point downward is the tenth [section], in which he commands Ānanda; first he is commanded, and finally he takes leave."
This is his name. Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi) in this language.
When Śākyamuni attained enlightenment, humans and devas celebrated with joy; he was born on that very night, and thus he was given this name.
Later, at the age of twenty, he finally left the household life.
He heard all the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma and served as the Buddha’s attendant; because he was both intimate with him and highly esteemed, the Buddha now summons him.
In the sutra, Ānanda went to visit him and inquire after his illness.
The commentary states:
"The concluding words are threefold; this [passage] generally expresses the exhaustion of one's arguments."

This means that the Buddha was indeed ill, and it was only then that I requested milk. He spoke of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the true Buddha has no illness, and he declined [the request] because his path was obstructed. As for the passage from "Why is this so? up to "one should use cow's milk": The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, why is this so? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should give a gift of food to all sentient beings. Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that is not included within the five aggregates? Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, there is nothing whatsoever that is not included within the five aggregates. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, it is impermanent. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? That which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, it is suffering. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If one were to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as 'this is mine, this am I, this is my self,' would that be appropriate? Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One, it would not be appropriate. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, they are impermanent. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? That which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, it is suffering. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If one were to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as 'this is mine, this am I, this is my self,' would that be appropriate? Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One, it would not be appropriate. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, therefore, whatever form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that form should be seen with right wisdom, exactly as it is, as: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self. Subhūti, whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that consciousness should be seen with right wisdom, exactly as it is, as: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self. Subhūti, when a noble disciple sees things in this way with right wisdom, exactly as they are, he becomes weary of form, weary of feeling, weary of perception, weary of mental formations, and weary of consciousness. Being weary of them, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; through liberation, he knows: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no further state of existence. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the emptiness of form, in the emptiness of feeling, in the emptiness of perception, in the emptiness of mental formations, and in the emptiness of consciousness. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the eye, in the emptiness of the ear, in the emptiness of the nose, in the emptiness of the tongue, in the emptiness of the body, and in the emptiness of the mind. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of forms, in the emptiness of sounds, in the emptiness of odors, in the emptiness of tastes, in the emptiness of tangibles, and in the emptiness of mental objects. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of eye-consciousness, in the emptiness of ear-consciousness, in the emptiness of nose-consciousness, in the emptiness of tongue-consciousness, in the emptiness of body-consciousness, and in the emptiness of mind-consciousness. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of eye-contact, in the emptiness of ear-contact, in the emptiness of nose-contact, in the emptiness of tongue-contact, in the emptiness of body-contact, and in the emptiness of mind-contact. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of feeling born of eye-contact, in the emptiness of feeling born of ear-contact, in the emptiness of feeling born of nose-contact, in the emptiness of feeling born of tongue-contact, in the emptiness of feeling born of body-contact, and in the emptiness of feeling born of mind-contact. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the earth element, in the emptiness of the water element, in the emptiness of the fire element, in the emptiness of the wind element, in the emptiness of the space element, and in the emptiness of the consciousness element. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the dharma of conditioned phenomena and in the emptiness of the dharma of unconditioned phenomena. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the dharma of the past, in the emptiness of the dharma of the future, and in the emptiness of the dharma of the present. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the dharma of all Buddhas and in the emptiness of the dharma of all dharmas. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the dharma of the Tathāgata and in the emptiness of the dharma of the Arhat. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the dharma of the Pratyekabuddha and in the emptiness of the dharma of the Śrāvaka. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the emptiness of the dharma of the Bodhisattva and in the emptiness of the dharma of the Buddha. The commentary states:
The following clarifies the ultimate principle; first there is the inquiry, and subsequently the clarification.
Within the clarification, there are two parts:
First, his own circumstances are set forth; second, the words of others are revealed.
There are two parts to his own circumstances:
first, his need for milk due to illness; second, his subsequent begging for it.
Regarding this inquiry and the Buddha’s illness, milk should be used.
As for the manifestation of a minor ailment, the Buddha suffered from back pain on occasion; milk mixed with *bisa* (lotus root) can serve as a remedy.

The following explains the reason for the objection.
Regarding the meaning of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

it is not that all sentient beings will necessarily realize emptiness and yet fail to attain *nirvāṇa*. Emptiness, being devoid of the fruits of suffering, is itself called *nirvāṇa*, because the Buddha perceives the true nature of suchness (*tathatā*) as emptiness to be *nirvāṇa*.
The *Yingliyi* (Principles of Correct Reasoning) states:
"Parinirvāṇa" is translated here as "perfect quiescence.
There are four types of nirvāṇa:
First is *svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*, which refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as the characteristic of all phenomena.
Second is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which refers to the revealed truth when the causes of suffering have been exhausted.
Third is nirvana without remainder, which refers to the ultimate truth manifested by the exhaustion of the fruits of suffering.
Fourth is non-abiding nirvana, which refers to the ultimate truth realized through the transformation of great compassion and prajñā upon the exhaustion of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Now, the nature of purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is used to challenge the other three types of nirvāṇa.
The intent of this challenge is as follows:
it is not the case that all sentient beings are incapable of attaining parinirvāṇa, for the Buddha taught that *tathatā* (suchness) is the nirvāṇa of natural purity.
Since the nirvana of intrinsic purity is inherently possessed, how could the other three meanings not likewise exist when they are manifested?
The ancients said: "The Buddha-wisdom and sentient beings are ultimately quiescent."
The existence of inherent purity now means that one knows there will be the mark of nirvāṇa in the future.
Apart from this true thusness (tathatā), there is no need for further extinction, because it has already been extinguished.
The Sūtra says: "By the Buddha’s contemplation, he attains parinirvāṇa."
The commentary states:

Because the Buddha perceives that the nature of sentient beings is the principle of quiescent emptiness as the essence of nirvāṇa, he teaches that sentient beings should realize this empty *tathatā* as parinirvāṇa; therefore, both principles [of yours and] those of the Venerable One are equal.
The *Yuktiṣaṣṭikāvṛtti* states:

Because the Buddha perceives that the true nature (*tathatā*) of the fundamental nature is the essence of nirvāṇa, he says that sentient beings shall realize this *tathatā* and thereby attain the other three kinds of parinirvāṇa.
The Venerable One shall attain it, and sentient beings shall also attain it.
Since it is difficult to attain, we know that natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*) is more difficult than the other three types.

The two types of "self" and "dharmas" are the objects of views and the attachments grasped by them.

The two types of phenomena—self and dharmas—are restless phenomena that serve as the objects of all conceptual constructions; their nature is not tranquil.
Reality is not so; therefore, it is free from conceptual construction. All agitation, bondage, and conceptualization are forever stilled.
The old translation states, "Obstruction is bodhi," which refers precisely to this freedom from bondage, though its intended meaning is difficult to grasp.
By citing what is governed [by it], this bodhi is revealed as being free [from all things];
yet, there is no quiescence. The Sūtra says: "Vast is bodhi, because it is immeasurable.

Since all conceptual proliferation has been stilled and debate forever ceased, there is no sign of an object to be grasped or a subject that can realize it; this is the wisdom of bodhi.

The commentary states:
These two phrases indicate that wisdom relies upon suchness.
"Dharma" refers to qualities (guṇa), and "dhātu" refers to nature (prakṛti). Since it is the dharma-nature of qualities, it is therefore called the *dharmadhātu*.
Wisdom abides in the dharma-realm because it follows true suchness (tathatā) to its ultimate limit.

Not only is there no duality in principle, but wisdom (*jñāna*) is likewise non-dual, for it is free from the conceptualized distinctions of imputed phenomena.

It has two parts:
The first two phrases clarify the essence of the bodhi of cessation;
the latter three phrases clarify the function of the bodhi of wisdom.

Sūtra: “Thorough knowledge is bodhi... up to: because it is not intermingled. Commentary:
The final three phrases clarify the function of wisdom and bodhi.

To universally know the activities of the mind is the function of illumination; right wisdom is precisely the gateway through which this is realized, for apart from this, there is no other faculty capable of such realization.

It is inseparable from the essence of the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); arising in dependence upon these six bases and being able to cognize all phenomena is what is called a "gate," for there is no gate other than this.

The fruit-wisdom is capable of convergence, whereas the causal six sense-bases are not capable of such convergence.

True reality (*tattva*), however, is not like this: it is manifested solely by names, and since sound possesses no functional activity, it cannot cause the essence and function of true reality to increase. Therein exists only a provisional name, devoid of any referential characteristic.
The older term "provisional name" (jiaming) carries a slightly different meaning; it is not like the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), which can be grasped or abandoned.
Just as waves are conditioned and subject to movement, the ultimate truth cannot be grasped or abandoned, and is therefore called "waveless."

In each pore of the World-Honored One’s body grows a single hair, soft, lustrous, deep blue-black, and curling to the right; this is the eleventh mark.

The tips of the World-Honored One’s body hairs all point upward, curling to the right, soft, lustrous, and deep blue-black, adorning his golden-hued body which is most lovely and delightful; this is the twelfth mark.
The Blessed One’s skin is fine, thin, and smooth; dust, grime, water, and the like do not adhere to it—this is the thirteenth [mark].

The Blessed One’s skin is entirely of a true golden color, brilliant and radiant like a sublime golden pedestal, adorned with various jewels, and a sight that all delight in beholding—this is the fourteenth [mark].
The World-Honored One’s two feet, two hands, palms, throat, and both shoulders are fully developed in seven places; this is the fifteenth.
The World-Honored One’s shoulders and neck are perfectly rounded and exquisite; this is the sixteenth.
The space between the Lord’s shoulders and armpits is completely filled; this is the seventeenth.
The Lord’s countenance is perfectly full, upright, and straight; this is the eighteenth.
The Lord’s physical form is tall, broad, and dignified; this is the nineteenth.
The Blessed One’s physical proportions are equal in length and breadth, perfectly symmetrical and complete like those of a *nyagrodha* tree; this is the twentieth.
The Blessed One’s chest and upper body possess a majestic presence as vast as that of a lion king; this is the twenty-first.
The World-Honored One’s constant radiance extends one fathom in every direction; this is the twenty-second.
The World-Honored One’s forty teeth are even and level, pure and closely set with deep roots, and whiter than white jade or snow; this is the twenty-third.
The Blessed One’s four canine teeth are brilliant white and sharp; this is the twenty-fourth.

The Blessed One always obtains the supreme taste among all tastes because his throat channels are straight; thus, he can draw up the various channels of the body's limbs and joints, and no superior flavors can be corrupted by disorders of wind, heat, or phlegm.

Because these are not corrupted, the channels are free from faults such as sinking, floating, stretching, contracting, damage, or crookedness; he is able to swallow correctly, and saliva flows freely through the channels, whereby body and mind are at ease and he constantly obtains the supreme taste—this is the twenty-fifth.
Twenty-sixth: The Blessed One’s tongue is thin, pure, broad, and long; it can cover his face up to the ears and the hairline. Twenty-seven:

The Blessed One’s Brahma-voice is harmonious and elegant; regardless of the number of listeners, all hear it equally, its resonance shaking like a celestial drum, and his speech is graceful and refined like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
The Blessed One’s eyelashes are like those of a bull king—deep blue, even, and not disordered; this is the twenty-eighth.
The Blessed One’s eyes are deep blue with a bright white sclera, adorned with a crimson ring, pure and clearly defined; this is the twenty-ninth.
The World-Honored One’s facial orb is like the full moon, and the mark of his eyebrows is bright and pure, like the bow of Śakra; this is the thirtieth.

Between the World-Honored One’s eyebrows is the mark of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which curls to the right and is as soft as *tūla* cotton; it is fresh, white, and pure, surpassing white jade, snow, and the like; this is the thirty-first.
The *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the World-Honored One’s head is lofty, prominent, and perfectly circular, like a great canopy;
this is the thirty-second. Subhūti, these are called the thirty-two marks of a Great Being.
"Subhūti! What are the eighty minor marks of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? Subhūti!"
The World-Honored One’s fingernails and toenails are narrow, long, thin, and supple; they are lustrous, pure, and bright, like red copper—this is the first.
The World-Honored One’s fingers and toes are rounded, slender, and long; they are smooth, straight, and soft, with the joints and bones not visible—this is the second.
The Blessed One’s hands and feet are each equal and without disparity, with all the spaces between the fingers and toes being completely filled and dense; this is the third [mark].
The Blessed One’s hands and feet are perfectly rounded and as one desires, soft, pure, and lustrous, with a color like that of a lotus; this is the fourth [mark].
The World-Honored One’s sinews and veins are coiled and knotted, firm and solid, deeply hidden and not visible; this is the fifth.
Both of the World-Honored One’s ankles are concealed and not visible; this is the sixth.
The World-Honored One’s gait is straight, steady, and deliberate, like that of a dragon-elephant king; this is the seventh.
The World-Honored One’s gait is majestic and dignified, like that of a lion king; this is the eighth.
The Blessed One’s gait is steady, composed, neither excessive nor deficient, like that of a bull king; this is the ninth.
The Blessed One’s manner of advancing and halting is elegant and graceful, like that of a swan king; this is the tenth.
The World-Honored One always turns his gaze to the right, like a royal elephant, with his entire body following the turn; this is the eleventh.
The joints and limbs of the World-Honored One are gradually rounded and well-proportioned, beautifully and skillfully arranged; this is the twelfth.
The Blessed One’s joints are interlocked without gaps, like the coils of a dragon; this is the thirteenth.
The Blessed One’s kneecaps are exquisitely well-placed, firm, and perfectly rounded; this is the fourteenth.
The private parts of the World-Honored One are well-concealed, with exquisite patterns, endowed with majestic power, perfect and pure; this is the fifteenth.
The limbs and members of the World-Honored One’s body are moist, supple, radiant, fresh, and clean, such that dust and grime do not adhere to them; this is the sixteenth.
The Blessed One’s physical presence is dignified and majestic, free from fear, and he is never timid or weak;
this is the seventeenth. The Blessed One’s limbs are firm and dense, well-knit and closely joined; this is the eighteenth.
The limbs of the Blessed One’s body are stable, firm, and never flickering; they are perfectly complete and without flaw—this is the nineteenth.
The physical marks of the Blessed One are like those of a royal seer; they are majestic on all sides, radiant and pure, free from any obscuration—this is the twentieth.
The Blessed One’s body is surrounded by a circular halo that constantly illuminates him during activities such as walking; this is the twenty-first.
The Blessed One’s abdomen is square and well-proportioned, soft and unprotuberant, adorned with all the marks; this is the twenty-second.
The World-Honored One’s navel is deep, spiraling to the right, perfectly round and exquisite, pure and lustrous; this is the twenty-third.
The World-Honored One’s navel is thick, neither sunken nor protruding, and its circumference is exquisitely beautiful; this is the twenty-fourth.
The Blessed One’s skin is free from scabies and eczema, and he is without blemishes, moles, warts, or other such defects; this is the twenty-fifth.
The Blessed One’s hands and feet are full and soft, and the soles of his feet are level; this is the twenty-sixth.
The World-Honored One’s hands have fingers that are deeply joined, long, bright, straight, moist, and unbroken; this is the twenty-seventh.
The color of the World-Honored One’s lips is lustrous and crimson, like the *bimba* fruit, with the upper and lower lips being perfectly proportioned; this is the twenty-eighth.
The Blessed One’s face is neither too long nor too short, neither too large nor too small; it is perfectly proportioned and majestic—this is the twenty-ninth.
The Blessed One’s tongue is soft, thin, broad, and long, with the color of red copper—this is the thirtieth.
The World-Honored One’s voice is majestic and its resonance reaches far and wide, like the roar of an elephant king; it is bright, clear, and penetrating—this is the thirty-first.
The World-Honored One’s vocal tones are exquisite and complete, like an echo from deep within a mountain valley—this is the thirty-second.
The World-Honored One’s nose is high, long, and straight, with no visible nostrils; this is the thirty-third.
All of the World-Honored One’s teeth are even, square, and brilliant white; this is the thirty-fourth.
The Blessed One’s teeth are rounded, white, and lustrous, and their edges are sharp; this is the thirty-fifth.
The Blessed One’s eyes are pure, with the blue and white clearly distinguished; this is the thirty-sixth.
The Blessed One’s eyes are long and wide, like the petals of a blue lotus, and are most lovely to behold; this is the thirty-seventh.
The Blessed One’s eyelashes are even above and below, thick and dark, not white; this is the thirty-eighth.
The World-Honored One’s eyebrows are long and not white, dense yet fine and soft; this is the thirty-ninth mark.
The World-Honored One’s eyebrows are elegant and well-ordered, the color of deep blue lapis lazuli; this is the fortieth mark.
The World-Honored One’s eyebrows are high, prominent, radiant, and smooth, shaped like the crescent moon; this is the forty-first.
The World-Honored One’s ears are thick, broad, long, and well-proportioned, with the circular lobes fully developed; this is the forty-second.
The World-Honored One’s two ears are beautiful and perfectly symmetrical, free from all defects; this is the forty-third [mark].
The World-Honored One’s deportment causes those who see him to be neither harmed nor defiled, but to give rise to love and respect; this is the forty-fourth [mark].
The Blessed One’s forehead is broad, full, level, and even; his physical form is exceptionally sublime—this is the forty-fifth.
The Blessed One’s upper body is perfectly developed, like that of a lion king; his majestic dignity is peerless—this is the forty-sixth.
The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is long, deep blue-black, fine and dense, and not white; this is the forty-seventh.
The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is fragrant and pure, fine and soft, lustrous, and curling; this is the forty-eighth.
The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is even and orderly without disorder, nor is it entangled; this is the forty-ninth.
The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is firm and unbroken, never falling out; this is the fiftieth.
The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is smooth, lustrous, and exquisite, with no dust or grime adhering to it;
this is the fifty-first. The World-Honored One’s body is firm and full, surpassing that of Nārāyaṇa; this is the fifty-second.
The Blessed One’s body is tall, large, and upright; this is the fifty-third.
The Blessed One’s assembly is pure and perfect; this is the fifty-fourth.
The Blessed One’s physical limbs possess preeminent power, with none equal to him; this is the fifty-fifth.
The physical marks of the World-Honored One are such that all who behold them find joy and never tire of gazing; this is the fifty-sixth.
The World-Honored One’s face is long and broad, perfectly proportioned, pure and radiant, like the full moon in autumn; this is the fifty-seventh.
The World-Honored One’s countenance is serene and radiant; he speaks with a smile and always faces others rather than turning his back—this is fifty-eight.
The World-Honored One’s face is lustrous and joyful, free from frowns or any discoloration such as blueness or redness—this is fifty-nine.
The skin of the Blessed One’s body is pure and stainless, and it is forever free from any unpleasant odor; this is the sixtieth.
From all the pores of the Blessed One’s body, there constantly issues a subtle and wondrous fragrance that fulfills all wishes; this is the sixty-first.
The World-Honored One’s face constantly emits the most supreme and excellent fragrance; this is the sixty-second.
The World-Honored One’s head is perfectly round and exquisite, and the Tathāgata’s *uṣṇīṣa* is like a celestial canopy; this is the sixty-third.

The World-Honored One’s body hairs are deep blue-black, radiant and pure, like the stalks of a *kuśa* reed; they are adorned with a crimson luster and are also copper-colored—this is the sixty-fourth.
The World-Honored One’s Dharma-voice accords with the capacity of the assembly, neither increasing nor decreasing, responding to principle without error—this is the sixty-fifth.
The crown of the World-Honored One’s head cannot be seen by anyone; this is the sixty-sixth.
The webbing between the fingers and toes of the World-Honored One is distinct, beautifully adorned, and the color is like that of red copper; this is the sixty-seventh.
When the World-Honored One walks, his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground, yet they leave imprints; this is sixty-eight.
The World-Honored One maintains himself without relying on others for protection; his body is without tilting or swaying; this is sixty-nine.
The World-Honored One’s majestic virtue resounds far and wide, such that those with evil minds see joy and those who are terrified find peace; this is the seventieth.
The World-Honored One’s voice is neither too high nor too low, conforming to the inclinations of sentient beings as he speaks to them with harmony and cheer; this is the seventy-first.
Seventy-second: The World-Honored One is able to preach the Dharma in accordance with the speech and mental inclinations of all classes of sentient beings. Seventy-third:
When the World-Honored One expounds the True Dharma with a single voice, each class of sentient beings understands it according to their own capacity.
The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma always follows a sequential order; there must be causes and conditions for it, and his words are never unwholesome—this is seventy-four.
The World-Honored One regards all classes of sentient beings with equanimity, praising the good and censuring the evil without affection or aversion—this is seventy-five.
The Blessed One acts only after first observing; his conduct is complete, causing beings to recognize and become pure—this is seventy-six.
No sentient being is able to fully perceive all the marks and signs of the Blessed One—this is seventy-seven.
The cranial bone of the World-Honored One is firm, solid, and perfectly rounded; this is the seventy-eighth.
The countenance of the World-Honored One is eternally youthful and does not age; he delights in visiting former places; this is the seventy-ninth.

On the hands, feet, and chest of the World-Honored One, there are all the auspicious marks of the *śrīvatsa* (the mark of excellence), with patterns as fine and complete as brocade and a color like vermilion; this is the eightieth.
"Subhūti! These are called the eighty minor marks. Subhūti!"

Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished such marks and secondary characteristics, the radiance of his body spontaneously illuminates the trichiliocosm, pervading it entirely without exception.
When he directs his attention, he is able to universally illuminate immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable worlds;
yet, out of compassion for all sentient beings, he withdraws the light so that it constantly shines from each face at a distance of one fathom.

If he were to emit his bodily radiance, all the light of the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies would be perpetually eclipsed; consequently, sentient beings would be unable to distinguish day from night, the waxing and waning phases of the moon, the days, months, and years, and their various undertakings would fail to reach completion.
The Buddha’s voice spontaneously pervades the trichiliocosm; yet when he directs his attention, it can fill immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable worlds.
Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, my voice accords with the capacity of the assembly, neither diminishing nor increasing. Subhūti!

Such meritorious benefits and advantages were already accomplished by me previously while practicing the perfection of wisdom in my bodhisattva stage; therefore, I am now adorned with the perfection of the primary and secondary marks, so that all sentient beings who see me rejoice and all obtain supreme benefit and peace.
"So it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to gather in all sentient beings through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma. This is a most marvelous and rare phenomenon."
Therefore, being endowed with the primary and secondary marks is called "peaceful bliss" (*sukha*).
If these various characteristics are deficient, it is not called bliss.
Cultivating these causal practices is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Sūtra: Reaching the sublime Bodhi, one observes bliss. Commentary:
These five fruits of adornment first adorn Bodhi, intended for the ascent to perfect enlightenment;
Second, they are not startled by the profound Dharma, being able both to receive it and to expound it;
third, they correctly contemplate the gates of liberation, being able both to cultivate them and to realize them;
fourth, they take nirvana as their object of focus and aspire to enter it—this last point is absent from the older translations.

Fifth, when observing sentient beings, one never acts at an improper time; rather, one exhorts and benefits them according to their capacity when the time is right. As for "improper time," it means not going to provide instruction or benefit to those whose faculties and capacities are not yet ready.
Therefore, the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma is free from four faults:
first, no inappropriate place; second, no inappropriate time; third, no inappropriate recipient; and fourth, no non-Dharma. Sūtra:
Among those of similar kind, he produces the joy of supreme bliss and the joy of protection.
The commentary states:
Sixth, there are seven benefits consisting of benefiting others and benefiting oneself, which are superior to harming others and oneself.
The first four benefit others; the latter three benefit oneself.
This is for the benefit of others.

Regarding those born of a similar class—those of the same type as those who have emerged into the supramundane holy life—one always delights in associating with them upon seeing their virtues, and one feels no increased aversion toward seeing those of a different class.
One should delight in associating with virtuous friends because it increases one's wholesome qualities;
one should guard against evil friends so that no transgressions arise.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The characteristics of a virtuous friend are: being without breach or flaw in ethical discipline, possessing extensive learning, having realized through cultivation, being compassionate, being fearless, being patient and untiring, and having clear and eloquent speech."

Seeking to bestow gifts, benefit, and happiness, possessing clear comprehension regarding this, endowed with power and skillful means, providing aid without abandoning others, and possessing unimpeded great compassion—such a person is called a virtuous friend.

His actions are never in vain; his deportment is perfect; his words and conduct are earnest and dignified; he is free from hypocrisy and envy; he is frugal and does not hoard what is excessive, relinquishing it as needed; he admonishes and reminds others of their lapses; he provides instruction and exhortation, and is able to preach the Dharma for them—such a person is called a virtuous friend and may be relied upon with trust.

Whether they are ill or healthy, one serves them with love and respect; one inquires after their well-being and greets them with prostrations; one cultivates the practice of harmony and reverence; one provides the four requisites and various articles without fail according to the season; and when attending to the business of respectful service, one listens attentively without distraction—this is called "intimate association."
Therefore, in this state, one delights in the joy of intimacy.
Sūtra: Through skillful means, one attains the most supreme and wondrous bliss. Commentary:
These three constitute self-benefit:
first, being well-ensconced within the twelve kinds of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), which is not present in the older translations;
second, rejoicing in and having faith in the true Dharma, and delighting in seeking to know it.
Third, non-negligence: constantly exhorting oneself to diligently cultivate the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) is the supreme [practice].
Sūtra: "Thus, sisters, you should not delight in sensual pleasures."
The commentary states:
This concludes the third discourse within the "Discourse on the Heavenly Maidens.
This is the joy of the Dharma-garden, wherein Bodhisattvas dwell eternally. One should take delight in this joy rather than in the pleasures of desire; thus, they are exhorted.
Sūtra: After some time, the evil Māra arrived and returned together with them to his celestial palace.
The commentary states:
This is the third section from below, clarifying the return to the palace.

This section consists of eight parts: first, summoning the daughter back to the palace; second, the daughter’s refusal to go; third, Māra’s request for her hand; fourth, Vimaladattā’s giving her away; fifth, the heavenly maidens’ inquiry; sixth, Vimaladattā’s explanation; seventh, the heavenly maidens’ prostration and thanks; eighth, the lifting of the restriction and the release of Māra.
This is the first passage of the text.
The Sūtra states: "The women replied... until 'we shall return with you.
The Commentary says:
The two daughters declined to leave.
This section has three parts:
first, a general refusal; second, an exposition of their reasoning; and third, the manifestation of their joy.
This is the initial general statement of the Sūtra.
Regarding the passage from "Why is this so? up to "I shall return with you," the Commentary says:
This explains the principle of not departing.
Since I have already come under the authority of another, I cannot go back against him.
Sūtra: "We shall now return; you may go back alone."
The commentary says:
This reveals the Dharma of bliss; therefore, one cannot turn back.
Scripture: At that time, the evil Māra, the enemy, approached the Mahāsattva.
The commentary states:
As for the three māras, he requested them as alms.
Because his mind was free from attachment and he had abandoned stinginess and greed, he was a great bodhisattva.
Sūtra: Vimalakīrti said, "Until the fulfillment of the vow for the Dharma.
Commentary: This refers to the four kinds of stainless giving.
A Mahāsattva accords with the wishes of sentient beings; because he now accords with them, he practices relinquishment.
Since this relinquishment is itself a practice, he then makes a vow: "May the vows for wholesome dharmas be fulfilled for you and all sentient beings."
Birth and death involve faults, and thus one's vows remain unfulfilled.
Because faultless, supreme vows cause all to be fulfilled, the sutra says:
"At that time, the celestial maidens arrived and asked: 'How should one practice?'"
The commentary states:
The five goddesses inquire about the Dharma.
From the words of Vimalakīrti in the sutra down to "you all should learn" [is the response].
The commentary states:
There are three points explained regarding the six kinds of stainlessness.
This consists of three parts: first, a brief exposition; second, a further inquiry; and third, an explanation.
This is the first part.
Because he wishes to ensure that the transmission of the Dharma does not cease, he speaks of the "inexhaustible lamp."
In order to cause them to seek out and hear the Dharma with earnest devotion, the sutra provides this brief explanation.
[The text] continues: "The heavenly maiden asked again, up to the point concerning the 'inexhaustible lamp.
The commentary states:
The second [point] is again an inquiry.
The Sūtra says: “The sisters replied... up to ‘there is also no retreating or hiding.
The Commentary says:
The third [section] is the explanation.
It has two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the exhortation.
The explanation consists of three parts:
first, the analogy; second, the mind; and third, the conclusion.
This is the analogy.
"Darkness" means obscurity.
The new light is not exhausted, and the old light does not diminish.
Sūtra: "Thus, sisters, it increases further and further."
The commentary states:
This clarifies the mind.
It is the hundred billion *koṭis* and the thousand billion *nayutas*.
The Bodhisattva’s transformation of these things establishes enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva’s mind of the Way has no end, for it arises ever more and more;
nor does it diminish, for it truly increases.
This is the exhortation to arouse the mind of enlightenment.
The Sūtra says: "In this way, for the sake of others, one reaches [the goal] and never again experiences decline.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the Dharma.
If the correct teaching of the Dharma is applied, the teaching will further increase;
it shall ultimately never be exhausted, nor will it diminish at the outset.
"Exhaustion" means total absence; "diminution" means reduction.
This is the exhortation to practice the Dharma.
Sūtra: "Sisters, you should know... up to "...you should train yourselves. This is the exhortation.
The commentary states:
The following exhorts others to practice.
First, the exhortation is established; finally, the virtues are revealed.
This is the exhortation.
The Sūtra says: "Though dwelling in the palace of Māra... up to all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
This reveals the virtue of cultivation.
To exhort those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment] is precisely to recognize the Buddha’s grace and virtue over many kalpas, which constitutes true repayment.
The fulfillment of one's own practice for self-benefit is also the bringing of benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; this is the virtue of benefiting others.
Sūtra: These goddesses approached Vimalakīrti. Commentary:
The seven goddesses paid their respects and offered thanks.
Having heard the Way so deeply, I offer my prostrations and thanks from the summit of my head.
After some time, Vimalakīrti returned to his own palace.
The commentary says:

Regarding the eighth [point], he relinquished his restraint of Māra and allowed him to return. Previously, through the power of his supernormal faculties, he had restrained him so that he could not return.
Now that his teaching of benefits was complete, he therefore relinquished his former restraint.
Sūtra: The World-Honored One went to him to inquire about his illness.
Commentary: The concluding words below are a response consisting of a humble request for leave to withdraw.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Volume Four, Part One.
